CORPORATION'S ANNUAL REPORT TO SHAREHOLDERS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Innovations, Inc.

CORPORATION'S ANNUAL REPORT TO SHAREHOLDERS — WHAT THIS INFORMATION SHEET COVERS
This information sheet addresses a specific, recurring statutory duty that runs from Acme Innovations, Inc.'s board of directors to its own shareholders: the duty, under California Corporations Code § 1501, to send an annual financial report. This is different from several other topics addressed elsewhere in this corpus. A shareholder's or member's statutory right to inspect and copy a corporation's books, records, and minutes (Corporations Code §§ 1600-1603) is a demand-driven right the shareholder exercises; § 1501 instead obligates the board to send a report on its own initiative, without waiting for any shareholder to ask. This is also different from the specialized annual reporting statutes this corpus describes for two particular corporate subtypes: the Benefit Corporation's annual benefit report and the Social Purpose Corporation's annual report with its special purpose management discussion and analysis are separate statutes, layered on top of (or, for the Social Purpose Corporation, expressly cross-referencing) the general rule this information sheet describes, and neither of those documents states what § 1501 itself requires of an ordinary corporation that is not organized under either of those specialized statutes. This document states what § 1501 requires; it does not tell Acme Innovations, Inc. or Taylor Morgan what to do about any specific fiscal year's report.

THE BOARD'S DUTY TO SEND AN ANNUAL REPORT WITHIN 120 DAYS — CORPORATIONS CODE § 1501(A)(1)
Corporations Code § 1501(a)(1) imposes an affirmative duty on the board itself, not merely a right a shareholder must invoke: "The board shall cause an annual report to be sent to the shareholders not later than 120 days after the close of the fiscal year, unless in the case of a corporation with less than 100 holders of record of its shares (determined as provided in Section 605) this requirement is expressly waived in the bylaws." The same paragraph fixes the report's minimum content: "This report shall contain a balance sheet as of the end of that fiscal year and an income statement and a statement of cashflows for that fiscal year, accompanied by any report thereon of independent accountants or, if there is no report, the certificate of an authorized officer of the corporation that the statements were prepared without audit from the books and records of the corporation." For Acme Innovations, Inc., whose fiscal year ends December 31, 2026, this section supplies the deadline and the minimum content that any report sent under it must contain, subject to the waiver and small-corporation provisions described in this document's companion clauses.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The board shall cause an annual report to be sent to the shareholders not later than 120 days after the close of the fiscal year, unless in the case of a corporation with less than 100 holders of record of its shares (determined as provided in Section 605) this requirement is expressly waived in the bylaws."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1501(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Corp. Code § 1501(a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1501.)
  "This report shall contain a balance sheet as of the end of that fiscal year and an income statement and a statement of cashflows for that fiscal year, accompanied by any report thereon of independent accountants or, if there is no report, the certificate of an authorized officer of the corporation that the statements were prepared without audit from the books and records of the corporation."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1501(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Corp. Code § 1501(a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1501.)
  Known gap: This clause states only what § 1501(a)(1) itself says about the duty, the 120-day deadline, and minimum content; it does not restate the small-corporation waiver mechanics or the separate GAAP exception (both addressed in this document's companion clauses), and it does not address what happens if a corporation with 100 or more holders of record attempts to waive the requirement by bylaw — the waiver is textually available only to a corporation with fewer than 100 holders of record. This is the current statutory text of § 1501(a)(1), fetched directly from the California Legislative Information website and verified byte-identical across two separate fetches using two distinct User-Agent strings. A CourtListener case-law search for judicial decisions construing this subdivision returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit error (125/day quota already exhausted) before any search could run; this clause and its companions therefore rest on the statutory text alone, with no case law verified for this document.

THE REPORT MAY BE SENT BY ELECTRONIC TRANSMISSION — CORPORATIONS CODE § 1501(A)(1)
The same subdivision that creates the annual report duty also authorizes one specific method of sending it: "Unless otherwise provided by the articles or bylaws and if approved by the board of directors, that report and any accompanying material sent pursuant to this section may be sent by electronic transmission by the corporation (Section 20)." For Acme Innovations, Inc., this means the board's approval — and the absence of a contrary provision in the articles or bylaws — are both preconditions to sending the report and any accompanying material electronically rather than by mail.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Unless otherwise provided by the articles or bylaws and if approved by the board of directors, that report and any accompanying material sent pursuant to this section may be sent by electronic transmission by the corporation (Section 20)."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1501(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Corp. Code § 1501(a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1501.)
  Known gap: This clause states only what § 1501(a)(1)'s electronic-transmission sentence itself says; it does not independently examine Section 20, the cross-referenced definition of "electronic transmission by the corporation," which was not separately fetched or quoted for this clause, so this clause does not state what that definition itself requires (for example, any recipient-consent or delivery-confirmation mechanics Section 20 may impose). This is the current statutory text of § 1501(a)(1), fetched directly from the California Legislative Information website and verified byte-identical across two separate fetches using two distinct User-Agent strings. No CourtListener case-law search could be completed for this clause; the daily quota (125/day) was already exhausted when checked.

TIMING RELATIVE TO THE ANNUAL MEETING — CORPORATIONS CODE § 1501(A)(2)
Beyond the 120-day outer deadline, § 1501(a)(2) ties the report's timing to the corporation's next annual shareholders' meeting: "Unless so waived, the report specified in paragraph (1) shall be sent to the shareholders at least 15 (or, if sent by third-class mail, 35) days before the annual meeting of shareholders to be held during the next fiscal year, but this requirement shall not limit the requirement for holding an annual meeting as required by Section 600." This means Acme Innovations, Inc.'s board must account for its method of delivery — ordinary mail, third-class mail, or another method — in calculating how far in advance of the annual meeting the report must go out, where the small-corporation waiver described elsewhere in this section does not apply.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Unless so waived, the report specified in paragraph (1) shall be sent to the shareholders at least 15 (or, if sent by third-class mail, 35) days before the annual meeting of shareholders to be held during the next fiscal year, but this requirement shall not limit the requirement for holding an annual meeting as required by Section 600."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1501(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), Corp. Code § 1501(a)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1501.)
  Known gap: This clause states only the timing rule in § 1501(a)(2); it does not restate the small-corporation waiver mechanics (addressed in this document's companion clause on § 1501(a)(1)) or the separate annual-meeting requirement in Section 600, which the quoted text cross-references but which this clause does not independently examine or quote. A RELAXED ACCOUNTING STANDARD FOR CORPORATIONS WITH FEWER THAN 100 HOLDERS — CORPORATIONS CODE § 1501(A)(3)
Section 1501(a)(3) provides a distinct accounting-standard exception, separate from the bylaw waiver described elsewhere in this section: "Notwithstanding Section 114, the financial statements of any corporation with fewer than 100 holders of record of its shares (determined as provided in Section 605) required to be furnished by this subdivision and subdivision (c) are not required to be prepared in conformity with generally accepted accounting principles if they reasonably set forth the assets and liabilities and the income and expense of the corporation and disclose the accounting basis used in their preparation." For a corporation such as Acme Innovations, Inc. with fewer than 100 holders of record, this exception applies whether or not the corporation has also exercised the separate bylaw waiver of the report itself — the two provisions address different questions.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Notwithstanding Section 114, the financial statements of any corporation with fewer than 100 holders of record of its shares (determined as provided in Section 605) required to be furnished by this subdivision and subdivision (c) are not required to be prepared in conformity with generally accepted accounting principles if they reasonably set forth the assets and liabilities and the income and expense of the corporation and disclose the accounting basis used in their preparation."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1501(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text), Corp. Code § 1501(a)(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1501.)
  Known gap: This clause states only what § 1501(a)(3) itself says; it does not independently examine Section 114 (the general financial-statement definition this subdivision displaces) or Section 605 (the cross-referenced method for determining who counts as a "holder of record"), neither of which was separately fetched or quoted for this clause. This exception governs only the accounting standard used to prepare the statements — it does not excuse a corporation from sending the report at all; that separate question is governed by the bylaw waiver described in this document's companion clause on § 1501(a)(1). This is the current statutory text of § 1501(a)(3), fetched directly from the California Legislative Information website and verified byte-identical across two separate fetches using two distinct User-Agent strings. ADDITIONAL DISCLOSURE FOR MID-SIZE CORPORATIONS: RELATED-PARTY TRANSACTIONS OVER $40,000 — CORPORATIONS CODE § 1501(B)(1)
For a corporation that is neither small enough to fall under the waiver described elsewhere in this section nor already subject to federal securities reporting, § 1501(b) adds two further disclosure items to the annual report: "In addition to the financial statements required by subdivision (a), the annual report of any corporation having 100 or more holders of record of its shares (determined as provided in Section 605) either not subject to the reporting requirements of Section 13 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, or exempted from those reporting requirements by Section 12(g)(2) of that act, shall also describe briefly both of the following:" The first of these, § 1501(b)(1), requires disclosure of certain related-party transactions: "Any transaction (excluding compensation of officers and directors) during the previous fiscal year involving an amount in excess of forty thousand dollars ($40,000) (other than contracts let at competitive bid or services rendered at prices regulated by law) to which the corporation or its parent or subsidiary was a party and in which any director or officer of the corporation or of a subsidiary or (if known to the corporation or its parent or subsidiary) any holder of more than 10 percent of the outstanding voting shares of the corporation had a direct or indirect material interest, naming the person and stating the person’s relationship to the corporation, the nature of the person’s interest in the transaction and, where practicable, the amount of the interest; provided that in the case of a transaction with a partnership of which the person is a partner, only the interest of the partnership need be stated; and provided further that no report need be made in the case of any transaction approved by the shareholders (Section 153)." This disclosure duty exists independently of, and describes a different thing than, the statutory self-dealing safe-harbor procedures this corpus's separate Self-Dealing and Interested Director/Officer Transactions document addresses under Corporations Code § 310 — this § 1501(b)(1) provision is a reporting obligation, not a procedure for validating the underlying transaction.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]

  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1501(b) (California Legislative Information text), Corp. Code § 1501(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1501.)
  "Any transaction (excluding compensation of officers and directors) during the previous fiscal year involving an amount in excess of forty thousand dollars ($40,000) (other than contracts let at competitive bid or services rendered at prices regulated by law) to which the corporation or its parent or subsidiary was a party and in which any director or officer of the corporation or of a subsidiary or (if known to the corporation or its parent or subsidiary) any holder of more than 10 percent of the outstanding voting shares of the corporation had a direct or indirect material interest, naming the person and stating the person’s relationship to the corporation, the nature of the person’s interest in the transaction and, where practicable, the amount of the interest; provided that in the case of a transaction with a partnership of which the person is a partner, only the interest of the partnership need be stated; and provided further that no report need be made in the case of any transaction approved by the shareholders (Section 153)."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1501(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Corp. Code § 1501(b)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1501.)
  Known gap: This clause states only what § 1501(b) and § 1501(b)(1) themselves say; it applies only to a corporation with 100 or more holders of record that is not already subject to, or exempted under Section 12(g)(2) from, federal Exchange Act reporting — it does not apply to a corporation that has waived the underlying annual report under the small-corporation provision described in this document's companion clause, nor to a corporation already filing under federal securities law. The $40,000 threshold and the cross-referenced Sections 13, 12(g)(2), and 153 were not independently fetched or verified as part of this clause; this clause states only what § 1501(b)(1)'s own text says about them. ADDITIONAL DISCLOSURE FOR MID-SIZE CORPORATIONS: INDEMNIFICATION OVER $10,000 — CORPORATIONS CODE § 1501(B)(2)
The second item § 1501(b) requires of a qualifying mid-size, non-SEC-reporting corporation's annual report concerns indemnification payments: "The amount and circumstances of any indemnification or advances aggregating more than ten thousand dollars ($10,000) paid during the fiscal year to any officer or director of the corporation pursuant to Section 317; provided that no report need be made in the case of indemnification approved by the shareholders (Section 153) under paragraph (2) of subdivision (e) of Section 317." This is a disclosure duty about indemnification payments already made — it describes a different question than the corpus's separate Director and Officer Indemnification document, which addresses the substantive Section 317 standards governing when and how a corporation may or must indemnify an agent in the first place.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The amount and circumstances of any indemnification or advances aggregating more than ten thousand dollars ($10,000) paid during the fiscal year to any officer or director of the corporation pursuant to Section 317; provided that no report need be made in the case of indemnification approved by the shareholders (Section 153) under paragraph (2) of subdivision (e) of Section 317."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1501(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text), Corp. Code § 1501(b)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1501.)
  Known gap: This clause states only what § 1501(b)(2) itself says; like the related-party transaction disclosure in this document's companion clause, it applies only to a corporation with 100 or more holders of record that is not already subject to, or exempted under Section 12(g)(2) from, federal Exchange Act reporting (the qualifying condition is stated in § 1501(b)'s introductory text, quoted in that companion clause, not repeated in this clause's own quoted text). This clause does not independently restate or verify what Section 317 itself provides about when indemnification is proper — that substantive standard is addressed in this corpus's separate Director and Officer Indemnification document. This is the current statutory text of § 1501(b)(2), fetched directly from the California Legislative Information website and verified byte-identical across two separate fetches using two distinct User-Agent strings. No CourtListener case-law search could be completed for this clause; the daily quota (125/day) was already exhausted when checked.

A SHAREHOLDER'S RIGHT TO DEMAND STATEMENTS WHEN NO REPORT WAS SENT — CORPORATIONS CODE § 1501(C)
Section 1501(c) gives an individual shareholder, such as Jordan Lee, a fallback right to demand financial statements when the board did not send the annual report: "If no annual report for the last fiscal year has been sent to shareholders, the corporation shall, upon the written request of any shareholder made more than 120 days after the close of that fiscal year, deliver or mail to the person making the request within 30 days thereafter the financial statements required by subdivision (a) for that year." The same subdivision gives a larger holding group a separate, broader right to more current interim financial information: "A shareholder or shareholders holding at least 5 percent of the outstanding shares of any class of a corporation may make a written request to the corporation for an income statement of the corporation for the three-month, six-month, or nine-month period of the current fiscal year ended more than 30 days before the date of the request and a balance sheet of the corporation as of the end of the period and, in addition, if no annual report for the last fiscal year has been sent to shareholders, the statements referred to in subdivision (a) for the last fiscal year."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "If no annual report for the last fiscal year has been sent to shareholders, the corporation shall, upon the written request of any shareholder made more than 120 days after the close of that fiscal year, deliver or mail to the person making the request within 30 days thereafter the financial statements required by subdivision (a) for that year."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1501(c) (California Legislative Information text), Corp. Code § 1501(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1501.)
  "A shareholder or shareholders holding at least 5 percent of the outstanding shares of any class of a corporation may make a written request to the corporation for an income statement of the corporation for the three-month, six-month, or nine-month period of the current fiscal year ended more than 30 days before the date of the request and a balance sheet of the corporation as of the end of the period and, in addition, if no annual report for the last fiscal year has been sent to shareholders, the statements referred to in subdivision (a) for the last fiscal year."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1501(c) (California Legislative Information text), Corp. Code § 1501(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1501.)
  Known gap: This clause states only what § 1501(c)'s two quoted sentences say; it does not restate the remainder of subdivision (c), which separately requires the resulting statements to be delivered or mailed within 30 days and kept on file at the principal office for 12 months, nor subdivision (d)'s requirement that any such quarterly statements be accompanied by an accountant's report or officer's certificate. This is a written-demand right exercised by the shareholder — it does not describe a right the corporation must satisfy without a request, which is instead the board's affirmative duty addressed in this document's companion clause on § 1501(a)(1). This is the current statutory text of § 1501(c), fetched directly from the California Legislative Information website and verified byte-identical across two separate fetches using two distinct User-Agent strings. No CourtListener case-law search could be completed for this clause; the daily quota (125/day) was already exhausted when checked.

COURT ENFORCEMENT AND FEE-SHIFTING FOR AN UNJUSTIFIED FAILURE TO REPORT — CORPORATIONS CODE § 1501(E)-(F)
Section 1501 backs its reporting duties with a specific court-enforcement mechanism. Subdivision (e) states: "In addition to the penalties provided for in Section 2200, the superior court of the proper county shall enforce the duty of making and mailing or delivering the information and financial statements required by this section and, for good cause shown, may extend the time therefor." Subdivision (f) then adds a discretionary fee-shifting remedy: "In any action or proceeding under this section, if the court finds the failure of the corporation to comply with the requirements of this section to have been without justification, the court may award an amount sufficient to reimburse the shareholder for the reasonable expenses incurred by the shareholder, including attorney’s fees, in connection with the action or proceeding."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "In addition to the penalties provided for in Section 2200, the superior court of the proper county shall enforce the duty of making and mailing or delivering the information and financial statements required by this section and, for good cause shown, may extend the time therefor."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1501(e) (California Legislative Information text), Corp. Code § 1501(e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1501.)
  "In any action or proceeding under this section, if the court finds the failure of the corporation to comply with the requirements of this section to have been without justification, the court may award an amount sufficient to reimburse the shareholder for the reasonable expenses incurred by the shareholder, including attorney’s fees, in connection with the action or proceeding."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1501(f) (California Legislative Information text), Corp. Code § 1501(f) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1501.)
  Known gap: This clause states only what subdivisions (e) and (f) themselves say; it does not independently examine Section 2200, the separate penalty provision subdivision (e) cross-references, which was not fetched or quoted for this clause. The fee award under subdivision (f) is discretionary ("may award") and conditioned on the court finding the corporation's noncompliance to have been "without justification" — a standard this section does not itself further define, and this clause does not predict how a court would apply it to any particular set of facts. This is the current statutory text of § 1501(e) and (f), fetched directly from the California Legislative Information website and verified byte-identical across two separate fetches using two distinct User-Agent strings. No CourtListener case-law search could be completed for this clause; the daily quota (125/day) was already exhausted when checked.

WHICH CORPORATIONS THIS SECTION REACHES — CORPORATIONS CODE § 1501(G)
Section 1501 is not limited to corporations formed in California. Subdivision (g) states its scope directly: "This section applies to any domestic corporation and also to a foreign corporation having its principal office in California or customarily holding meetings of its board in this state." For Acme Innovations, Inc., this means the analysis in this document's other clauses turns on where the corporation's principal office is located or where its board customarily meets, not solely on the state of incorporation named in its articles.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "This section applies to any domestic corporation and also to a foreign corporation having its principal office in California or customarily holding meetings of its board in this state."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 1501(g) (California Legislative Information text), Corp. Code § 1501(g) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=1501.)
  Known gap: This clause states only what § 1501(g) itself says; it does not independently examine how "customarily holding meetings of its board in this state" would be established or contested for a particular corporation, a term this subdivision does not further define. This clause also does not restate or cross-reference how this scope provision interacts with Corporations Code § 2115, the pseudo-foreign corporation statute this corpus's separate Section 2115 document addresses, which applies a different multi-factor test to determine which of California's corporate statutes reach an out-of-state corporation more generally — that document was not re-examined as part of this clause, and this clause does not claim the two statutes' scope tests are identical. This is the current statutory text of § 1501(g), fetched directly from the California Legislative Information website and verified byte-identical across two separate fetches using two distinct User-Agent strings. No CourtListener case-law search could be completed for this clause; the daily quota (125/day) was already exhausted when checked.

PREPARER ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Prepared for Acme Innovations, Inc., which reports 42 holders of record of its shares as of the date below. Prepared by: Taylor Morgan. Date: September 6, 2026. Signed at: Sacramento, California. This information sheet states facts about California Corporations Code § 1501's annual-report-to-shareholders requirements; it does not recommend or advise how Acme Innovations, Inc. should prepare, deliver, or respond to any specific fiscal year's report.

expectedJSON.body: Section 1501(c) gives an individual shareholder, such as Jordan Lee, a fallback right to demand financial statements when the board did not send the annual report: "If no annual report for the last fiscal year has been sent to shareholders, the corporation shall, upon the written request of any shareholder made more than 120 days after the close of that fiscal year, deliver or mail to the person making the request within 30 days thereafter the financial statements required by subdivision (a) for that year." The same subdivision gives a larger holding group a separate, broader right to more current interim financial information: "A shareholder or shareholders holding at least 5 percent of the outstanding shares of any class of a corporation may make a written request to the corporation for an income statement of the corporation for the three-month, six-month, or nine-month period of the current fiscal year ended more than 30 days before the date of the request and a balance sheet of the corporation as of the end of the period and, in addition, if no annual report for the last fiscal year has been sent to shareholders, the statements referred to in subdivision (a) for the last fiscal year."

expectedJSON.body: Section 1501 backs its reporting duties with a specific court-enforcement mechanism. Subdivision (e) states: "In addition to the penalties provided for in Section 2200, the superior court of the proper county shall enforce the duty of making and mailing or delivering the information and financial statements required by this section and, for good cause shown, may extend the time therefor." Subdivision (f) then adds a discretionary fee-shifting remedy: "In any action or proceeding under this section, if the court finds the failure of the corporation to comply with the requirements of this section to have been without justification, the court may award an amount sufficient to reimburse the shareholder for the reasonable expenses incurred by the shareholder, including attorney’s fees, in connection with the action or proceeding."
